decks.title: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio — Part 1: Sacrificing and Gaining Ratios, Goodwill
goals: Explain why existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio and what it sets off
Calculate each partner's sacrifice or gain and the sacrificing and gaining ratios, including surrender of a share
Pass the goodwill adjustment entry under AS 26, writing off any goodwill already in the books

slides.heading: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio among Existing Partners
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **sacrificing and gaining ratios** and the **goodwill adjustment**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why partners change their ratio, sacrificing and gaining shares, special cases, the goodwill adjustment under Accounting Standard 26, and goodwill already in the books
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Partners do not always share profits in the same ratio for ever. When one partner takes on more work or another steps back, they agree a new ratio. In this part we learn to measure exactly who gives up a share and who gains one, and how the gaining partners compensate the others for goodwill, following Accounting Standard twenty-six.

slides.heading: Why do partners change their ratio?
bullets: A partner takes on **more responsibility** or a new branch.
A partner gives **less time** because of age, health or another venture.
A change in **capital** or **skill** contributed.
No partner joins or leaves: the **same partners** reshare profits.

nodes.label: Past values settled in the old ratio (revaluation, reserves)

visual.alt: Flow: the partners agree a new ratio; some partners sacrifice and others gain; gainers compensate sacrificers for goodwill; and past values such as revaluation results and reserves are settled in the old ratio
visual.caption: What a change in ratio sets off

slides.narration: Ratios change for practical reasons. One partner may start running a new branch, while another may want to spend less time in the business. Whatever the reason, the same partners now reshare profits. This sets off a chain: some partners sacrifice, others gain, gainers pay for goodwill, and past gains and reserves are settled in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Sacrificing and gaining shares
bullets: **Sacrificing ratio** = old ratio − new ratio.
**Gaining ratio** = new ratio − old ratio.

rows: Left out of the goodwill entry

visual.alt: Table of formulas: a sacrificing share is old share minus new share, a gaining share is new share minus old share, and a partner whose share is unchanged is left out of the goodwill entry
visual.caption: Total sacrifice always equals total gain.

slides.narration: For each partner, subtract the new share from the old share. A positive answer is a sacrifice. A negative answer means the partner gains, and the gain is new share minus old share. If the answer is zero, the partner is unaffected. Because the same profit is shared among the same people, the total sacrificed always equals the total gained.

visual.alt: Grouped bar chart for an imagined firm of Meera, Naveen and Omkar: Meera falls from one half to two fifths, Naveen rises from three eighths to two fifths, and Omkar rises from one eighth to one fifth
visual.caption: Meera's bar falls (sacrifice); Naveen's and Omkar's rise (gains).

slides.narration: This chart shows an imagined tiffin service run by Meera, Naveen and Omkar. The light bars are the old shares and the dark bars the new shares. Meera's bar falls, so she sacrifices. Naveen's and Omkar's bars rise, so both of them gain. The fall in one bar is exactly matched by the rises in the others.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: three partners, different denominators
slides.body_md: Meera, Naveen and Omkar (an imagined tiffin service in Mumbai) share 4 : 3 : 1. New ratio 2 : 2 : 1. Find each partner's sacrifice or gain and the gaining ratio.
bullets: Step 1 — Write every share over a common denominator (40).
Step 2 — Old − new for each partner.
Step 3 — Read the signs; form the gaining ratio.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 1: over a denominator of forty, Meera goes from twenty to sixteen and sacrifices four fortieths, one tenth; Naveen goes from fifteen to sixteen and gains one fortieth; Omkar goes from five to eight and gains three fortieths
visual.caption: Gaining ratio Naveen : Omkar = 1 : 3

slides.narration: The old shares are in eighths and the new ones in fifths, so we use forty as the common denominator. Meera falls from twenty fortieths to sixteen, a sacrifice of four fortieths, or one tenth. Naveen rises from fifteen to sixteen, a gain of one fortieth. Omkar rises from five to eight, a gain of three fortieths. So the gaining ratio is one to three.

slides.heading: Quick check: is every partner affected?
slides.body_md: Think about a partner whose share does not change.
slides.narration: Imagine a partner whose old share and new share are exactly the same. Does that partner sacrifice anything, or gain anything?

slides.heading: Special cases

rows: Old − new for each partner, over a common denominator
A partner gives a fraction **of the firm's profit** to another
Subtract that fraction from the giver, add it to the taker
A partner gives a fraction **of his or her own share**
Fraction × own share = amount given; then adjust both
New share of each = 1 ÷ number of partners

visual.alt: Table of special cases: given both ratios, subtract; given a fraction of the firm's profit, move it directly; given a fraction of a partner's own share, multiply first; for equal sharing, each new share is one over the number of partners

slides.narration: Questions describe the change in different ways. Sometimes both ratios are given; just subtract. Sometimes a partner gives a fraction of the firm's profit; move that fraction directly. Be careful when a partner gives a fraction of his or her own share: multiply it by that share first. And when partners agree to share equally, each new share is one over the number of partners.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: surrender of part of a share
slides.body_md: Tara and Uday (an imagined photo studio in Mangaluru) share 3 : 2. Tara surrenders one-third of her share to Uday. Find the new ratio.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: Tara surrenders one third of her three fifths, which is one fifth; her new share is two fifths and Uday's is three fifths, so the new ratio is two to three

slides.narration: Tara gives up one third of her own share. Her share is three fifths, so she gives one third of three fifths, which is one fifth. Her new share is three fifths minus one fifth, two fifths. Uday gets two fifths plus one fifth, three fifths. The new ratio is two to three. Notice that one third of her share is not one third of the firm's profit.

slides.heading: Quick check: new ratio from a sacrifice
slides.body_md: Is the fraction given out of the firm's profit or out of her own share?
slides.narration: Read the question slowly. The words of the firm's profit and of her share lead to different answers.

slides.heading: Goodwill on a change in ratio
bullets: The **gaining** partner will get more of future profits that the firm's reputation earns, so must **compensate** the sacrificing partner.
**AS 26:** only **purchased** goodwill is recorded; so **no goodwill account** is raised.

nodes.label: Find each partner's gain or sacrifice
Debit gainers, credit sacrificers (no goodwill account)

visual.alt: Flow of the goodwill adjustment: value the firm's goodwill, find each partner's gain or sacrifice, multiply the gain by goodwill, then debit the gaining partners and credit the sacrificing partners without opening a goodwill account
visual.caption: Accounting Standard 26: self-generated goodwill is never recorded

slides.narration: Goodwill is the value of the firm's reputation, which helps it earn future profits. When a partner gains a larger share, he or she will enjoy more of those profits, so the sacrificing partner must be compensated. Under Accounting Standard twenty-six, goodwill built up by the firm itself is never recorded. So we pass an adjustment entry between the partners' capital accounts instead.

slides.heading: The adjustment entry
bullets: Amount for each partner = **firm's goodwill × that partner's gain or sacrifice**.
Total debits = total credits, because total gain = total sacrifice.

rows: *(Being goodwill adjusted on change in ratio)*

visual.alt: Format of the adjustment entry: the gaining partner's capital account is debited with gain times goodwill, and the sacrificing partner's capital account is credited with sacrifice times goodwill

slides.narration: The entry is simple. Debit the capital account of each gaining partner with gain times goodwill. Credit the capital account of each sacrificing partner with sacrifice times goodwill. Because total gain equals total sacrifice, the entry always balances. A partner whose share has not changed does not appear in the entry at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: goodwill adjustment for three partners
slides.body_md: The tiffin service of Meera, Naveen and Omkar values its goodwill at ₹1,60,000. Pass the adjustment entry for the change to 2 : 2 : 1.

rows: *(Being Naveen and Omkar compensate Meera for goodwill in the gaining ratio 1 : 3)*

visual.alt: Journal entry of worked example 3: Naveen's capital is debited four thousand rupees and Omkar's twelve thousand, and Meera's capital is credited sixteen thousand rupees
visual.caption: Goodwill ₹1,60,000: Meera 1/10, Naveen 1/40, Omkar 3/40 of it

slides.narration: From worked example one, Meera sacrifices one tenth, Naveen gains one fortieth and Omkar gains three fortieths. One tenth of one lakh sixty thousand rupees is sixteen thousand, credited to Meera. Naveen pays one fortieth, four thousand rupees, and Omkar pays three fortieths, twelve thousand rupees. Debits of sixteen thousand equal the credit of sixteen thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: the goodwill entry
slides.body_md: Who pays, and who is paid?
slides.narration: Remember: the partner who gets more of the future profit pays the partner who gives it up.

slides.heading: Goodwill already in the books
bullets: First **write off** the existing goodwill in the **old ratio**.
Then pass the adjustment entry for the **current value** of goodwill.

rows: Goodwill already in the balance sheet
All Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c
Gaining Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs

visual.alt: Table: goodwill already in the books is written off against all partners in the old ratio; goodwill valued now is adjusted between gaining and sacrificing partners; with fixed capitals the same entries pass through current accounts

slides.narration: Sometimes the balance sheet already shows goodwill from an earlier purchase. This old figure is written off among all partners in the old ratio, because it belongs to the old arrangement. Then the goodwill valued today is adjusted between gainers and sacrificers in the usual way. If capitals are fixed, the same entries pass through the partners' current accounts.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: existing goodwill and a new valuation
slides.body_md: The studio of Tara and Uday shows goodwill of ₹30,000. On the change to 2 : 3, goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000. Pass the entries.

rows: *(Being goodwill of the Mangaluru studio written off by Tara and Uday in 3 : 2)*
*(Being Uday's 1/5 gain of goodwill credited to Tara)*

visual.alt: Journal entries of worked example 4: first Tara and Uday write off old goodwill of thirty thousand rupees, eighteen thousand and twelve thousand; then Uday's capital is debited and Tara's credited twenty thousand rupees

slides.narration: First, write off the thirty thousand rupees of old goodwill in the old ratio of three to two: eighteen thousand to Tara and twelve thousand to Uday. Next, Tara sacrifices one fifth and Uday gains one fifth. One fifth of one lakh rupees is twenty thousand, so Uday's capital is debited and Tara's capital credited with twenty thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Fixed capitals and other details
bullets: **Fixed capitals:** all adjustments go through **current accounts**.
Goodwill is often valued first by **average profit** or **super profit** (Chapter 1 methods); then the same entry applies.
Never credit goodwill to **all** partners in the new ratio: that would raise a goodwill account.
slides.narration: Two details complete the picture. If the partnership deed fixes the capitals, every adjustment goes through current accounts instead. And the goodwill figure may first have to be worked out by the average profit or super profit method from chapter one. After that, the adjustment entry is passed in exactly the same way.

slides.heading: Quick check: old goodwill
slides.body_md: In which ratio is goodwill already in the books written off?
slides.narration: Think about when the old goodwill was acquired, and which ratio applied then.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: No goodwill account; gainers Dr., sacrificers Cr.
Written off in the old ratio

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: sacrifice is old minus new, gain is new minus old, total sacrifice equals total gain, goodwill is adjusted by debiting gainers and crediting sacrificers, old goodwill is written off in the old ratio, and fixed capitals use current accounts

slides.narration: To sum up: a sacrifice is old share minus new share and a gain is new share minus old share, and the two totals are always equal. Watch the wording in special cases. Under Accounting Standard twenty-six no goodwill account is raised: gaining partners are debited and sacrificing partners credited. Goodwill already in the books is first written off in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always show shares over a **common denominator** before subtracting.
A fraction **of a partner's share** must be multiplied by that share first.
Name the partner who is **not affected**: examiners look for it.
Goodwill entry: **gainers Dr., sacrificers Cr.**, with a narration.
Write off **existing goodwill** before adjusting the new value.
slides.narration: Some advice for the board exam. Show every share over a common denominator before you subtract. Watch for a fraction of a partner's own share. When one partner is unaffected, say so clearly. Write the goodwill entry with gainers debited, sacrificers credited, and a short narration. And if goodwill already appears in the books, write it off first, in the old ratio.

decks.title: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio — Part 2: Revaluation, Reserves and Accumulated Profits
goals: Prepare a revaluation account and share its gain or loss in the old ratio
Distribute general reserve, profit and loss balances, workmen compensation reserve and investment fluctuation reserve
Pass a single adjustment entry when partners keep book values and reserves unchanged

slides.heading: Revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits
slides.body_md: Part 2 — settling the **past** in the **old ratio** before the new ratio begins.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why assets and liabilities are revalued, the revaluation account, reserves and accumulated profits, the workmen compensation and investment fluctuation reserves, and the single adjustment entry
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we settled goodwill. But the balance sheet also carries assets at old values and reserves built from past profits. All of these belong to the period of the old ratio. In this part we revalue assets and liabilities, distribute reserves and accumulated profits or losses, deal with two special reserves, and learn a shortcut entry for when the books are not to be disturbed.

slides.heading: Why revalue on a change in ratio?
bullets: Assets may be worth more or less than their **book values**; some liabilities may be **unrecorded**.
If not settled now, the gain or loss would later be shared in the **new ratio**, which is unfair.

nodes.label: Book values are out of date
Gain or loss arose under the old ratio
Settle it now in the old ratio
Future changes shared in the new ratio

visual.alt: Flow: book values are out of date; the gain or loss arose under the old ratio; it is settled now in the old ratio; and future changes are shared in the new ratio
visual.caption: Fairness between the partners

slides.narration: Book values drift away from real values. Land rises, machines fall, and some liabilities are never recorded. These gains and losses happened while the old ratio applied. If we left them in the books, they would later be shared in the new ratio, and the gaining partners would benefit unfairly. So we revalue now and share the result in the old ratio.

slides.heading: The revaluation account
slides.body_md: A **nominal account**: gains on the credit side, losses on the debit side; the balance goes to the partners' capital accounts in the **old ratio**.

rows: Increase in a liability (or new provision)

visual.alt: Table of revaluation rules: increases in assets, decreases in liabilities and unrecorded assets are credited; decreases in assets, increases in liabilities or provisions and unrecorded liabilities are debited; the balance is shared in the old ratio

slides.narration: The revaluation account collects every change in value. An increase in an asset, a decrease in a liability or an unrecorded asset is a gain, so it is credited. A decrease in an asset, a new provision or an unrecorded liability is a loss, so it is debited. The balance, profit or loss, is transferred to the partners in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Quick check: credit or debit?
slides.body_md: Gains are credited; losses are debited.
slides.narration: For each option, ask: does this make the owners richer or poorer? Richer means a credit to the revaluation account.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: revaluation account
slides.body_md: Lata and Mohan (an imagined hardware wholesaler in Ludhiana) share 3 : 2 and change to 1 : 1. Building (₹2,00,000) up 20%; machinery (₹1,50,000) down 10%; provision on debtors of ₹80,000 raised from ₹1,000 to 5%; outstanding wages ₹2,000 to be recorded.

visual.alt: Revaluation account of worked example 5: debit side machinery fifteen thousand, provision three thousand, outstanding wages two thousand, and the gain of twenty thousand rupees split twelve thousand to Lata and eight thousand to Mohan; credit side building forty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Gain ₹20,000 shared 3 : 2

slides.narration: The building rises by twenty per cent of two lakh rupees, forty thousand, a credit. Machinery falls by fifteen thousand, a debit. The new provision is four thousand, but one thousand already exists, so only three thousand is debited. The unrecorded wages of two thousand are debited too. The gain of twenty thousand rupees is shared three to two: twelve thousand to Lata and eight thousand to Mohan.

slides.heading: Journal entries for revaluation
bullets: Increase in asset: **Asset A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c**.
Decrease in asset or new liability: **Revaluation A/c Dr. To Asset or Liability A/c**.
Gain: **Revaluation A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs** (old ratio).

rows: To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c

visual.alt: Journal entries for worked example 5: building debited and revaluation credited forty thousand; revaluation debited twenty thousand for machinery, provision and outstanding wages; and revaluation debited twenty thousand with Lata credited twelve thousand and Mohan eight thousand

slides.narration: The revaluation account is built from journal entries. Debit the building and credit revaluation for the rise. Debit revaluation and credit machinery, the provision and outstanding wages for the losses. Finally, close the account by transferring the gain to the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. A loss would be closed the other way round.

slides.heading: Reserves and accumulated profits or losses

rows: Credited to partners in the **old ratio**
Credited to partners in the **old ratio**
Debited to partners in the **old ratio**
Claim provided first; excess to partners (old ratio)
Fall in investments met first; excess to partners (old ratio)

visual.alt: Table of treatments: general and contingency reserves and a credit balance of profit and loss are credited to partners in the old ratio; a debit balance of profit and loss is debited in the old ratio; the workmen compensation reserve first meets the claim and the investment fluctuation reserve first meets the fall in investments, with any excess to the partners in the old ratio

slides.narration: Reserves and the balance of the profit and loss account were built from past profits, or show past losses. If the partners do not want them in the books, they are transferred to the capital accounts in the old ratio. A general reserve or a credit balance is credited to the partners. A debit balance, which is an accumulated loss, is debited to them.

slides.heading: Quick check: general reserve
slides.body_md: Which ratio applies to profits of the past?
slides.narration: Ask yourself when the general reserve was built, and which ratio applied at that time.

slides.heading: Workmen compensation reserve

rows: WCR A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio)
WCR A/c Dr. To Provision for WC Claim A/c (claim), To Partners' Capital A/cs (excess)
WCR A/c Dr. To Provision for WC Claim A/c
WCR A/c Dr. (reserve) + Revaluation A/c Dr. (excess) To Provision for WC Claim A/c

visual.alt: Table of workmen compensation reserve cases: no claim, the whole reserve goes to partners; claim less than reserve, the claim goes to a provision and the excess to partners; claim equal to reserve, all to the provision; claim more than reserve, the excess is debited to the revaluation account
visual.caption: WCR = workmen compensation reserve; WC = workmen compensation

slides.narration: A workmen compensation reserve is kept for claims by workers. First provide for any expected claim. If the claim is smaller than the reserve, the claim goes to a provision and the rest goes to the partners in the old ratio. If the claim is larger than the reserve, the whole reserve is used and the extra amount is a loss, debited to the revaluation account.

slides.heading: Investment fluctuation reserve

rows: IFR A/c Dr. To Investments A/c (fall), To Partners' Capital A/cs (rest)
IFR A/c Dr. (all) + Revaluation A/c Dr. (excess fall) To Investments A/c
Investments A/c Dr. To Revaluation A/c (rise); whole IFR to partners

visual.alt: Table of investment fluctuation reserve cases: at book value the whole reserve goes to partners; a fall up to the reserve is absorbed and the rest goes to partners; a fall larger than the reserve is absorbed up to the reserve and the excess is a revaluation loss; a rise is a revaluation gain and the whole reserve goes to partners
visual.caption: IFR = investment fluctuation reserve

slides.narration: An investment fluctuation reserve protects against a fall in the value of investments. If investments have fallen, the fall is met from this reserve first, and any balance goes to the partners. If the fall is bigger than the reserve, the excess is a revaluation loss. If investments have risen, the rise is a revaluation gain and the whole reserve goes to the partners.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: reserves of Lata and Mohan
slides.body_md: General reserve ₹50,000; profit and loss credit ₹20,000; workmen compensation reserve ₹15,000 with a claim of ₹6,000; investment fluctuation reserve ₹10,000 with investments of ₹60,000 now worth ₹56,000. Old ratio 3 : 2.

rows: To Provision for Workmen Compensation Claim A/c

visual.alt: Journal entries of worked example 6: general reserve fifty thousand and profit and loss twenty thousand credited to Lata forty-two thousand and Mohan twenty-eight thousand; workmen reserve fifteen thousand split into a six thousand provision and nine thousand to the partners; investment reserve ten thousand split into four thousand for the fall in investments and six thousand to the partners

slides.narration: The general reserve and the profit balance together make seventy thousand rupees, shared three to two. The workmen reserve of fifteen thousand first provides six thousand for the claim, and nine thousand goes to the partners. Investments have fallen by four thousand, so the investment reserve of ten thousand absorbs that fall and the remaining six thousand goes to the partners.

slides.heading: Quick check: workmen compensation reserve
slides.narration: Subtract the expected claim from the reserve. Only what is left belongs to the partners.

slides.heading: Keeping the books unchanged: one adjustment entry
bullets: Used when partners want **book values** and **reserves** to stay as they are.
Amount for each partner = **net accumulated profits × sacrifice or gain**.

nodes.label: Add reserves, accumulated profits and the net revaluation result
Total × each partner's sacrifice or gain
One entry: gainers Dr., sacrificers Cr.
Book values and reserves stay as they are

visual.alt: Flow of the single adjustment entry: add the reserves, accumulated profits and the net revaluation result; multiply the total by each partner's sacrifice or gain; pass one entry debiting gainers and crediting sacrificers; book values and reserves stay unchanged
visual.caption: Used when partners do not want to alter the books

notes.title: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio among Existing Partners — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and effects of a change in ratio
sections.body_md:
Existing partners may agree a **new profit-sharing ratio** without anyone joining or leaving, for example when a partner takes on more work, gives less time, or contributes more capital or skill. The change is a **reconstitution** of the firm.

It sets off four adjustments:
1. Some partners **sacrifice** and others **gain**.
2. Gainers **compensate** sacrificers for **goodwill**.
3. Assets and liabilities are **revalued**, and the gain or loss is shared in the **old ratio**.
4. **Reserves** and **accumulated profits or losses** are distributed in the **old ratio** (or one adjustment entry is passed).

key_terms.definition_md: A change in the agreement among partners, such as a new profit-sharing ratio.
The ratio in which partners share profits and losses.

nodes.label: Past values settled in the old ratio (revaluation, reserves)

visual.alt: Flow: the partners agree a new ratio; some partners sacrifice and others gain; gainers compensate sacrificers for goodwill; and past values such as revaluation results and reserves are settled in the old ratio
visual.caption: What a change in ratio sets off

sections.heading: 2. Sacrificing and gaining ratios
sections.body_md:
- **Sacrifice** of a partner = **old share − new share** (when positive).
- **Gain** of a partner = **new share − old share** (when positive).
- **Sacrificing ratio**: ratio of the sacrifices; **gaining ratio**: ratio of the gains.
- A partner with old share = new share is **unaffected**.
- **Check:** total sacrifice = total gain.

**Special cases**
- A fraction **of the firm's profit** is given: subtract it from the giver, add it to the taker.
- A fraction **of a partner's own share** is given: multiply it by that share first.
- **Equal sharing**: each new share = 1 ÷ number of partners.

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio in which partners give up their shares; old ratio − new ratio.
The ratio in which partners acquire additional shares; new ratio − old ratio.

sections.heading: 3. Goodwill under AS 26
sections.body_md:
**Accounting Standard 26 (Intangible Assets):** goodwill is recorded **only when purchased** for a consideration. Goodwill generated by the firm itself is **never** recorded, so no goodwill account is raised on a change in ratio.

**Adjustment entry:**

| Particulars | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|
| Gaining Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. | gain × goodwill | |
| To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs | | sacrifice × goodwill |

- Goodwill may first be valued by the **average profit**, **super profit** or **capitalisation** method (Chapter 1).
- A partner whose share is unchanged does **not** appear in the entry.

key_terms.definition_md: The value of a firm's reputation that enables it to earn more than normal profits.
An entry between partners' capital (or current) accounts that compensates sacrificing partners without opening a goodwill account.

sections.heading: 4. Existing goodwill and fixed capitals
sections.body_md:
- **Goodwill already in the balance sheet** is written off among **all** partners in the **old ratio**: Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c.
- Then the **current value** of goodwill is adjusted between gaining and sacrificing partners.
- If capitals are **fixed**, every adjustment (goodwill, reserves, revaluation) passes through the partners' **current accounts**.

key_terms.definition_md: Capital accounts show only the agreed capital; all other items go to current accounts.

sections.heading: 5. Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
sections.body_md:
Book values may differ from current values, and some assets or liabilities may be unrecorded. These changes arose under the **old ratio**, so they are settled before the new ratio begins.

- **Revaluation account** (a **nominal** account): gains credited, losses debited.
- Increase in an asset, decrease in a liability, unrecorded asset: **credit**.
- Decrease in an asset, increase in a liability or provision, unrecorded liability: **debit**.
- For a **provision for doubtful debts**, debit only the increase over the existing provision.
- **Balance** (profit or loss) to partners' capital accounts in the **old ratio**.

key_terms.definition_md: A nominal account that records increases and decreases in the values of assets and liabilities on reconstitution.
A liability that exists but is not in the books; bringing it in is a revaluation loss.

rows: Increase in a liability (or new provision)

sections.heading: 6. Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
sections.body_md:
- **General reserve**, **contingency reserve**, **profit and loss credit balance**: credited to partners in the **old ratio**.
- **Profit and loss debit balance**: debited to partners in the **old ratio**.
- **Workmen compensation reserve (WCR):** the expected claim is transferred to a **provision for workmen compensation claim**; any excess goes to partners; if the claim exceeds the reserve, the excess is **debited to revaluation**.
- **Investment fluctuation reserve (IFR):** a fall in investments is met from it first; any balance goes to partners; a fall larger than the reserve is a **revaluation loss**; a rise in value is a **revaluation gain** and the whole IFR goes to partners.

key_terms.definition_md: A reserve kept from profits to meet claims by workers for compensation.
A reserve kept to meet a fall in the market value of investments.
A debit balance of the profit and loss account carried in the balance sheet.

sections.heading: 7. Single adjustment entry when the books are unchanged
sections.body_md:
If partners want reserves and book values to stay unchanged:
1. Add reserves and accumulated profits, subtract accumulated losses, and add the **net revaluation result** (gain +, loss −).
2. Multiply the total by each partner's **sacrifice or gain**.
3. Pass **one entry**: Gaining Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs.

Goodwill can be included in the same total. Both methods leave each partner equally well off.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Sharing the revaluation result or a reserve in the **new** ratio instead of the old one.
- Treating a fraction **of a partner's share** as a fraction of the firm's profit.
- Opening a **goodwill account** at full value: AS 26 does not allow it for self-generated goodwill.
- Forgetting to write off **existing goodwill** in the old ratio before adjusting the new value.
- Debiting the **whole** new provision for doubtful debts instead of only the increase.
- Distributing the **whole** workmen compensation or investment fluctuation reserve when a claim or a fall must be met first.

**How marks are usually split**
- 1 mark: one correct option, ratio or amount.
- 3 marks: working (1), amounts (1), entry or account (1).
- 4 marks: valuation or revaluation working (1–2), ratio (1), entries (1–2).
- 6 marks: revaluation account (about 2), goodwill and reserves (about 2), capital accounts or balance sheet (about 2); step marks are given even if one figure slips.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: When existing partners change their profit-sharing ratio, the share sacrificed by a partner is calculated as

options.text_md: new share minus old share
old share minus new share
old share divided by new share
new share multiplied by old share

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** old share minus new share. A sacrifice is the part of the old share that a partner gives up, so it is old share − new share. New − old gives a gain.

questions.stem_md: Why is the sacrificing ratio worked out when the partners of a firm agree to a new profit-sharing ratio?

options.text_md: To fix the ratio in which the losses of earlier years will now be shared
To calculate interest on the partners' capitals for the year
To decide how much capital a new partner must bring
To find how much compensation each sacrificing partner should receive from the gaining partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To find how much compensation each sacrificing partner should receive from the gaining partners. The sacrificing partners give up future profits, so the gaining partners compensate them (mainly for goodwill). The sacrificing ratio tells how that compensation is shared. Past losses go in the old ratio, and no new partner is involved here.

questions.stem_md: Rhea and Sohan run an imagined bakery in Indore and share profits 3 : 2. From 1 April they agree to share profits equally. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Rhea sacrifices 1/10 and Sohan gains 1/10
Sohan sacrifices 1/10 and Rhea gains 1/10
Rhea sacrifices 1/5 and Sohan gains 1/5
Neither partner sacrifices, because the number of partners is the same

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rhea sacrifices 1/10 and Sohan gains 1/10. Rhea: 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10 (sacrifice). Sohan: 2/5 − 1/2 = −1/10 (gain). What Rhea gives up, Sohan takes.

questions.stem_md: Pranav, Qadir and Ruchi, partners in an imagined courier firm in Nagpur, share profits 4 : 3 : 2. They change the ratio to 2 : 3 : 4. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Pranav and Qadir sacrifice 2/9 each and Ruchi gains 4/9
Pranav sacrifices 2/9, and Qadir and Ruchi gain 1/9 each
Pranav sacrifices 2/9, Ruchi gains 2/9 and Qadir neither sacrifices nor gains
All three partners gain, because Ruchi's share has doubled

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Pranav sacrifices 2/9, Ruchi gains 2/9 and Qadir neither sacrifices nor gains. Over 9: Pranav 4/9 − 2/9 = 2/9 sacrificed; Qadir 3/9 − 3/9 = 0; Ruchi 2/9 − 4/9 = −2/9, a gain. Qadir is not affected.

questions.stem_md: Kiran, Latika and Manav share profits 5 : 3 : 2 in an imagined tailoring unit in Surat. Their new ratio is 2 : 5 : 3. The gaining ratio of Latika and Manav is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 2 : 1. Latika gains 5/10 − 3/10 = 2/10; Manav gains 3/10 − 2/10 = 1/10. Gaining ratio = 2 : 1 (Kiran sacrifices 3/10).

questions.stem_md: Varun and Wasim share profits 3 : 2 in an imagined travel agency in Shimla. Varun gives one-fifth of his share to Wasim. Their new profit-sharing ratio is
Esha and Farah share profits equally. Esha agrees to give up 1/10 of the firm's profit in favour of Farah. Their new ratio will be
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 2 : 3. Esha: 1/2 − 1/10 = 4/10; Farah: 1/2 + 1/10 = 6/10, so 2 : 3. (9 : 11 would be the answer if she gave 1/10 of her own share.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? When only the existing partners change their ratio, the total of the shares sacrificed equals the total of the shares gained.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The whole profit is still shared among the same partners, so every fraction given up by one partner is taken up by another.

questions.stem_md: True or false? On a change in the profit-sharing ratio, every partner of the firm must either make a sacrifice or make a gain.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A partner whose new share equals the old share is not affected: no sacrifice and no gain. Such a partner takes no part in the goodwill adjustment.

questions.stem_md: Gaining ratio = new ratio − ___ ratio.
questions.solution_md: A gain is the increase in share: new ratio − old ratio.

questions.stem_md: A partner whose new share is the same as the old share neither sacrifices nor ___.
questions.solution_md: Old share − new share = 0, so the partner neither sacrifices nor gains.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On a change in the profit-sharing ratio among existing partners, the sum of all sacrifices equals the sum of all gains.

**Reason (R):** The total profit is still divided among the same partners, so any share one partner gives up is taken by another partner.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true, and R gives the reason for A: with no outsider, a share given up can only go to another existing partner.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When two partners change their ratio from 1 : 1 to 3 : 2, both partners make a sacrifice.

**Reason (R):** A partner's sacrifice is measured as the old share minus the new share.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the first partner gains 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10 and the second sacrifices 1/10; both cannot sacrifice. R is a correct statement of the formula.

questions.stem_md: Neha and Om, partners in an imagined printing press in Bhopal, change their ratio from 3 : 2 to 2 : 3. The firm earns a profit of ₹1,80,000 in the first year after the change. By how much is Om's share of this profit higher than it would have been under the old ratio? (Answer in ₹.)

Arjun, Bela and Chirag run an imagined event-management firm in Lucknow, sharing profits 3 : 2 : 1. They decide to share future profits 2 : 2 : 1. Calculate each partner's sacrifice or gain, and the sacrificing and gaining ratios.
questions.solution_md: Bring old and new shares to one denominator (30), subtract, and read the signs.

answer.model_answer_md:
Common denominator 30:

| Partner | Old share | New share | Old − new | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arjun | 1/2 = 15/30 | 2/5 = 12/30 | 3/30 | Sacrifices 1/10 |
| Bela | 1/3 = 10/30 | 2/5 = 12/30 | −2/30 | Gains 1/15 |
| Chirag | 1/6 = 5/30 | 1/5 = 6/30 | −1/30 | Gains 1/30 |

- **Arjun is the only sacrificing partner** (1/10).
- Bela gains 1/15 (= 2/30) and Chirag gains 1/30.
- **Gaining ratio (Bela : Chirag) = 2 : 1**. Check: 2/30 + 1/30 = 3/30, equal to Arjun's sacrifice.

Sacrifice of Arjun and gains of Bela and Chirag

questions.stem_md: Dev, Gauri and Harsh are partners in an imagined solar-panel installation firm in Pune sharing profits 2 : 2 : 1. Dev wants to spend more time on another venture and surrenders one-fourth of his share, which Gauri and Harsh take equally. Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio and the gaining ratio.
questions.solution_md: Find the fraction surrendered, split it equally, add to the takers' old shares, then reduce.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Dev's share surrendered = 1/4 × 2/5 = **1/10**; Gauri and Harsh each take 1/20.
2. New shares: Dev 2/5 − 1/10 = **3/10**; Gauri 2/5 + 1/20 = **9/20**; Harsh 1/5 + 1/20 = **1/4**.
3. Over 20: 6/20, 9/20, 5/20 → **new ratio 6 : 9 : 5**.
4. Gains: Gauri 1/20, Harsh 1/20 → **gaining ratio 1 : 1**.

marking_scheme.step: New shares of all three partners

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the sacrificing ratio and the gaining ratio on three bases.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, formula and purpose, each contrasted in a table.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Sacrificing ratio | Gaining ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Ratio in which partners **give up** part of their shares | Ratio in which partners **acquire** additional shares |
| Formula | **Old ratio − new ratio** | **New ratio − old ratio** |
| Use | Shows how the **compensation received** (for goodwill) is shared among sacrificing partners | Shows how the **compensation paid** is shared among gaining partners |

questions.stem_md: Match each term in column I with its correct description in column II.

options.text_md: Sacrificing ratio
Gaining ratio
Revaluation account
Accounting Standard 26

match_right.text_md: Goodwill is recorded only when purchased for a consideration
Records changes in the values of assets and liabilities

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The two ratios are mirror images; the revaluation account carries changes in book values; AS 26 forbids recording self-generated goodwill.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a likely reason for the existing partners of a firm to change their profit-sharing ratio?

options.text_md: The firm has bought a new delivery van on credit
One partner will now give less time to the business because of other commitments
The bank has raised the interest rate on the firm's loan
A customer has paid an old debt that was overdue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** One partner will now give less time to the business because of other commitments. A change in the partners' roles, time, skill or capital is a reason to reshare profits. Buying an asset, a change in loan interest or the recovery of a debt are ordinary transactions.

questions.stem_md: According to Accounting Standard 26 (Intangible Assets), a firm may record goodwill in its books only when it is

options.text_md: purchased for a consideration in money or money's worth
valued by the partners at the time of a change in ratio
built up by the firm's own reputation over many years
agreed upon by a majority of the partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** purchased for a consideration in money or money's worth. Only purchased goodwill is recorded. Self-generated goodwill, even if the partners value it, is not raised in the books; its value is used only to pass the adjustment entry.

questions.stem_md: On a change in the profit-sharing ratio, the journal entry to adjust goodwill (no goodwill account in the books) is

options.text_md: Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Gaining partners' Capital A/cs
Gaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
Goodwill A/c Dr. To All partners' Capital A/cs (new ratio)
All partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c (new ratio)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Gaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs. The gaining partners pay for the extra share they receive, so their capitals are debited; the sacrificing partners are compensated, so their capitals are credited. No goodwill account is opened.

questions.stem_md: Goodwill already appearing in the balance sheet at the time the partners change their ratio is

options.text_md: written off among all the partners in their new ratio
kept in the books at its old value
written off among all the partners in their old ratio
credited to the gaining partners in their gaining ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** written off among all the partners in their old ratio. Old goodwill belongs to the period of the old ratio, so it is written off in that ratio: Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Goodwill A/c.

questions.stem_md: Ojas and Pia share profits 2 : 1 in an imagined pottery studio in Khurja and decide to share equally. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹90,000. The goodwill adjustment entry is for

options.text_md: ₹15,000, debited to Ojas and credited to Pia
₹30,000, debited to Pia and credited to Ojas
₹45,000, debited to Pia and credited to Ojas
₹15,000, debited to Pia and credited to Ojas

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹15,000, debited to Pia and credited to Ojas. Ojas sacrifices 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6; Pia gains the same. 90,000 × 1/6 = 15,000: Pia (gainer) is debited.

questions.stem_md: Asif, Bina and Chetan share profits 3 : 3 : 2 and change to 4 : 2 : 2. Goodwill is to be adjusted without opening a goodwill account. Whose capital account is NOT affected by the goodwill adjustment entry?

options.text_md: Asif's
Bina's
None: all three capital accounts are affected
Chetan's

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Chetan's. Over 8: Asif 3 → 4 gains 1/8, Bina 3 → 2 sacrifices 1/8, Chetan 2 → 2 no change. Only Asif (debited) and Bina (credited) appear in the entry.

questions.stem_md: Ritu and Sahil, partners in an imagined coaching centre in Kota, share profits 5 : 3. They decide to share profits equally from 1 April. The goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹2,40,000. By how much will Ritu's capital account be credited for goodwill? (Answer in ₹.)

Ishita, Jatin and Kunal own an imagined bicycle-repair chain in Chandigarh and share profits 3 : 2 : 1. They agree on a new ratio of 1 : 3 : 2 and value goodwill at ₹1,20,000. What total amount will be credited to Ishita's capital account for goodwill? (Answer in ₹.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ishita's sacrifice = 3/6 − 1/6 = 1/3; Jatin and Kunal gain 1/6 each.
Step 2: 1,20,000 × 1/3 = 40,000, paid 20,000 each by Jatin and Kunal. So ₹40,000.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under Accounting Standard 26, when partners change their ratio, a goodwill account is opened in the books at the full value of the firm's goodwill.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Self-generated goodwill cannot be recorded. The valuation is used only for an adjustment entry between the gaining and sacrificing partners' capital accounts.

questions.stem_md: Goodwill already shown in the balance sheet is written off among all the partners in their ___ ratio when the profit-sharing ratio changes.
questions.solution_md: It is written off in the old ratio, because it arose while the old ratio applied.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On a change in the profit-sharing ratio, the gaining partners compensate the sacrificing partners for their share of goodwill.

**Reason (R):** Goodwill is an intangible asset: it cannot be seen or touched.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. But the compensation is paid because the gainers will enjoy a larger share of future profits that goodwill helps earn, not because goodwill is intangible, so R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the partners' capitals are fixed, the goodwill adjustment on a change in ratio is made through their current accounts.

**Reason (R):** Accounting Standard 26 allows a firm to record goodwill that it has generated itself.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: under fixed capitals all adjustments go through current accounts. R is false: AS 26 permits only purchased goodwill to be recorded.

questions.stem_md: Kavya, Lalit and Mira are partners in an imagined organic-farm business near Nashik, sharing profits 5 : 3 : 2. From 1 April 2026 they will share 2 : 3 : 5. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. Pass the journal entry for goodwill, showing your working.
questions.solution_md: Find each partner's change, multiply the gain by goodwill, and debit the gainer to credit the sacrificer.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Partner | Old share | New share | Old − new | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kavya | 1/2 = 5/10 | 1/5 = 2/10 | 3/10 | Sacrifices 3/10 |
| Lalit | 3/10 | 3/10 | 0/10 | No change |
| Mira | 1/5 = 2/10 | 1/2 = 5/10 | −3/10 | Gains 3/10 |

Mira's gain 3/10 × 1,50,000 = **₹45,000**, paid to Kavya.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Mira's Capital A/c Dr. | 45,000 | |
| To Kavya's Capital A/c | | 45,000 |
| *(Being Mira's gain of 3/10 adjusted with Kavya on the change to 2 : 3 : 5)* | | |

Lalit's share is unchanged, so his capital is not affected.

marking_scheme.step: Sacrifice and gain worked out (Lalit unaffected)

questions.stem_md: Nikhil and Oorja run an imagined café in Kochi and share profits 3 : 1. Their balance sheet shows goodwill of ₹40,000. They now decide to share profits equally, and goodwill is valued at ₹80,000. Pass the necessary journal entries.
questions.solution_md: Write off the book goodwill in the old ratio first; then adjust the new valuation through the capital accounts.

answer.model_answer_md:
Nikhil sacrifices 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4; Oorja gains 1/4.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| (i) Nikhil's Capital A/c Dr. | 30,000 | |
| Oorja's Capital A/c Dr. | 10,000 | |
| To Goodwill A/c | | 40,000 |
| *(Being goodwill in the books of Nikhil and Oorja written off in the old ratio 3 : 1)* | | |
| (ii) Oorja's Capital A/c Dr. | 20,000 | |
| To Nikhil's Capital A/c | | 20,000 |
| *(Being Oorja's gain of 1/4 of goodwill of 80,000 credited to Nikhil)* | | |

marking_scheme.step: Existing goodwill written off in old ratio

questions.stem_md: Pallavi and Qasim are partners in an imagined software-testing firm in Hyderabad. Their capitals are fixed, and they share profits equally. They agree that from now on profits will be shared 3 : 2. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹2,10,000. Pass the journal entry and explain why the current accounts are used.
questions.solution_md: Gain × goodwill, gainer debited, sacrificer credited, using current accounts because capitals are fixed.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Pallavi: 1/2 − 3/5 = −1/10 (gain); Qasim: 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10 (sacrifice).
2. Amount = 2,10,000 × 1/10 = **₹21,000**.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Pallavi's Current A/c Dr. | 21,000 | |
| To Qasim's Current A/c | | 21,000 |
| *(Being Pallavi's 1/10 gain of goodwill compensated to Qasim)* | | |

3. With **fixed capitals**, capital accounts show only the agreed capital; every adjustment (goodwill, reserves, revaluation) passes through the **current accounts**.

marking_scheme.step: Correct entry through current accounts for 21,000

questions.stem_md: Sanjay, Tanvi and Uma share profits 2 : 2 : 1 in an imagined spice-export firm in Guntur. From 1 April 2026 they agree to share 3 : 1 : 1. Goodwill is to be valued at 2 years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years, which were ₹60,000, ₹80,000, ₹1,00,000. Calculate the goodwill and pass the journal entry for its adjustment.
questions.solution_md: Average the three profits, multiply by the years of purchase, then apply the gain or sacrifice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Average profit = (60,000 + 80,000 + 1,00,000) ÷ 3 = **₹80,000**.
2. Goodwill = 80,000 × 2 = **₹1,60,000**.
3. Changes over 5: Sanjay 2/5 → 3/5 gains 1/5; Tanvi 2/5 → 1/5 sacrifices 1/5; Uma 1/5 → 1/5 no change.
4. Amount = 1,60,000 × 1/5 = **₹32,000**.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sanjay's Capital A/c Dr. | 32,000 | |
| To Tanvi's Capital A/c | | 32,000 |
| *(Being Sanjay's gain of 1/5 of goodwill compensated to Tanvi)* | | |

questions.stem_md: Vikram, Wahida and Yash run an imagined handloom store in Varanasi and share profits 3 : 2 : 1. They decide to share profits equally in future. The firm's capital employed is ₹5,00,000, the normal rate of return in this business is 10% and the average profit is ₹80,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 3 years' purchase of super profit. Value the goodwill, identify the partners affected and pass the adjustment entry.
questions.solution_md: Super profit = average − normal; multiply by years of purchase; only the partners whose shares change enter the entry.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Normal profit = 5,00,000 × 10% = **₹50,000**; super profit = 80,000 − 50,000 = **₹30,000**.
2. Goodwill = 30,000 × 3 = **₹90,000**.
3. Over 6: Vikram 3/6 → 2/6 sacrifices 1/6; Wahida 2/6 → 2/6 unaffected; Yash 1/6 → 2/6 gains 1/6.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Yash's Capital A/c Dr. | 15,000 | |
| To Vikram's Capital A/c | | 15,000 |
| *(Being Yash's 1/6 gain of goodwill credited to Vikram; Wahida unaffected)* | | |

marking_scheme.step: Wahida identified as unaffected; Vikram and Yash shares

questions.stem_md: Zoya, Aman and Bhavna share profits 5 : 3 : 2 in an imagined interior-design firm in Jaipur. Bhavna has taken charge of the firm's new branch, so it is agreed that she will take 1/10 of the firm's profit from Zoya's share. Goodwill of ₹25,000 appears in the books, and the firm's goodwill is now valued at ₹2,00,000. Calculate the new ratio and pass the journal entries.
questions.solution_md: New ratio from the share taken; old goodwill written off in the old ratio; new goodwill adjusted for the 1/10 transfer.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. New shares: Zoya 5/10 − 1/10 = 2/5; Aman 3/10; Bhavna 2/10 + 1/10 = 3/10 → **new ratio 4 : 3 : 3**.
2. Only Zoya sacrifices (1/10) and only Bhavna gains (1/10).

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---:|---:|
| (i) Zoya's Capital A/c Dr. | 12,500 | |
| Aman's Capital A/c Dr. | 7,500 | |
| Bhavna's Capital A/c Dr. | 5,000 | |
| To Goodwill A/c | | 25,000 |
| *(Being old goodwill of the Jaipur firm written off in 5 : 3 : 2)* | | |
| (ii) Bhavna's Capital A/c Dr. | 20,000 | |
| To Zoya's Capital A/c | | 20,000 |
| *(Being Bhavna's 1/10 gain of goodwill of 2,00,000 credited to Zoya)* | | |

marking_scheme.step: Existing goodwill written off in old ratio

questions.stem_md: Why must a gaining partner compensate a sacrificing partner for goodwill when their ratio changes?

options.text_md: The gaining partner has to buy the firm's physical assets from the sacrificing partner
Goodwill must be shown in the balance sheet at its full value after every change
The gaining partner will now receive a larger share of future profits that the firm's established reputation helps to earn
The sacrificing partner is leaving the firm and must be paid off

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The gaining partner will now receive a larger share of future profits that the firm's established reputation helps to earn. Goodwill is the value of expected future super profits. A larger future share means the gainer acquires part of that value from the sacrificer, so compensation is due. No asset is sold and no partner leaves.

questions.stem_md: The revaluation account prepared on a change in the profit-sharing ratio is a

options.text_md: real account
nominal account
personal account
memorandum statement that is never closed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** nominal account. It records gains and losses from revaluing assets and liabilities and is closed by transferring its balance to the partners, so it is a nominal account.

questions.stem_md: On a change in the profit-sharing ratio among existing partners, a profit on revaluation is shared among the partners in their

options.text_md: old ratio
new ratio
sacrificing ratio
gaining ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** old ratio. The change in value took place while the old ratio applied, so the gain or loss belongs to the partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **credited** to the revaluation account?

options.text_md: A decrease in the value of furniture
An increase in the value of land
An unrecorded electricity bill now brought into the books
An increase in the provision for doubtful debts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An increase in the value of land. Gains are credited: a rise in an asset's value. A fall in an asset, a new liability and a larger provision are losses, so they are debited.

questions.stem_md: While changing their ratio, the partners find an outstanding salary bill that was never recorded. In the revaluation account, this bill is

options.text_md: credited, because liabilities appear on the right side of the balance sheet
ignored, because outstanding expenses are paid within the year
credited to the partners' capital accounts directly in the new ratio
debited, because a new liability reduces the firm's net worth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debited, because a new liability reduces the firm's net worth. Bringing in a liability is a loss to the owners, so it is debited to the revaluation account (Revaluation A/c Dr. To Outstanding Salary A/c).

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm's debtors are ₹1,00,000 and the existing provision for doubtful debts is ₹3,000. On a change in ratio, the partners decide to keep the provision at 5% of debtors. The effect on the revaluation account is

options.text_md: ₹2,000 debited
₹5,000 debited
₹2,000 credited
₹8,000 debited

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹2,000 debited. Required provision = 5% of 1,00,000 = 5,000; only the increase of 5,000 − 3,000 = 2,000 is a new loss, debited to revaluation.

questions.stem_md: Partners change their ratio and do not wish to keep the general reserve in the books. The general reserve is

options.text_md: transferred to the partners' capital accounts in the new ratio
transferred to the revaluation account
transferred to the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
kept in the books and shared in the gaining ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** transferred to the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. A reserve is profit set aside in earlier years, when the old ratio applied: General Reserve A/c Dr. To Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio).

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm has a workmen compensation reserve of ₹30,000. On a change in the partners' ratio, a claim of ₹12,000 is expected. The amount to be shared among the partners in their old ratio is

options.text_md: nil

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹18,000. The claim of 12,000 goes to a provision for the claim; the rest, 30,000 − 12,000 = 18,000, belongs to the partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: The workmen compensation reserve of an imagined firm is ₹20,000, and the claim on account of workmen compensation is ₹26,000. On a change in ratio, the revaluation account will be

options.text_md: debited by ₹6,000
credited by ₹6,000
debited by ₹26,000
not affected

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debited by ₹6,000. The reserve covers 20,000 of the claim; the shortfall of 26,000 − 20,000 = 6,000 is a loss, debited to revaluation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm holds investments with a book value of ₹1,00,000 and an investment fluctuation reserve of ₹15,000. On a change in ratio, the market value of the investments is ₹92,000. The amount credited to the partners' capital accounts out of this reserve is

options.text_md: nil

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹7,000. Fall in value = 1,00,000 − 92,000 = 8,000, met from the reserve; the balance 15,000 − 8,000 = 7,000 goes to the partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: A debit balance of the profit and loss account appearing in the balance sheet at the time of a change in ratio is

options.text_md: credited to all partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
debited to all partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
debited to all partners' capital accounts in the new ratio
debited to the revaluation account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** debited to all partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. It is an accumulated loss of the old-ratio period, so the partners bear it in the old ratio: Partners' Capital A/cs Dr. To Profit and Loss A/c.

questions.stem_md: Partners change their ratio but want the reserves and the book values of assets and liabilities to stay unchanged. They should

options.text_md: pass one adjustment entry, debiting the gaining partners and crediting the sacrificing partners for their share of the net accumulated profits
distribute the reserves in the new ratio and prepare a revaluation account
prepare a revaluation account and keep the reserves in the books
pass no entry, because nothing has changed in the books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** pass one adjustment entry, debiting the gaining partners and crediting the sacrificing partners for their share of the net accumulated profits. Without changing book figures, fairness is restored by one entry: net accumulated profits (or the would-be revaluation result) × each partner's sacrifice or gain.

questions.stem_md: On a change in the profit-sharing ratio of an imagined hardware store in Rajkot: the building is revalued upwards by ₹30,000; stock is reduced by ₹8,000; the provision for doubtful debts is raised by ₹2,500; an investment of ₹4,000 not recorded earlier is brought into the books; and outstanding rent of ₹1,500 is recorded. Find the profit on revaluation (in ₹).

Rajat, Seema and Tarun run an imagined printing unit in Sivakasi and share profits 2 : 2 : 1. They decide to share equally. On revaluation, machinery falls by ₹12,000, furniture falls by ₹6,000 and land rises by ₹3,000. What amount of the revaluation result is debited to Tarun's capital account? (Answer in ₹.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Net = 3,000 − (12,000 + 6,000) = −15,000, a loss.
Step 2: Shared in the old ratio 2 : 2 : 1, Tarun bears 1/5 × 15,000 = 3,000. So ₹3,000.

questions.stem_md: Uday and Vani share profits 3 : 1 in an imagined brick kiln near Meerut and are changing their ratio. The workmen compensation reserve is ₹40,000 and the expected claim is ₹16,000. How much will be credited to Uday's capital account from this reserve? (Answer in ₹.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Excess of reserve = 40,000 − 16,000 = 24,000.
Step 2: Uday's 3/4 share = 18,000. So ₹18,000.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm shows investments at ₹80,000 and an investment fluctuation reserve of ₹6,000. When the partners change their ratio, the investments are worth only ₹71,000. What amount will be debited to the revaluation account? (Answer in ₹.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Fall = 80,000 − 71,000 = 9,000.
Step 2: The reserve absorbs 6,000; the rest, 9,000 − 6,000 = 3,000, is a revaluation loss. So ₹3,000.

questions.stem_md: Xavier and Yamini share profits 3 : 2 in an imagined dairy in Anand and change to 2 : 3. Their books show a general reserve of ₹60,000 and a credit balance of ₹15,000 in the profit and loss account, which they wish to keep in the books. For what amount will the single adjustment entry be passed? (Answer in ₹.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Accumulated profits kept = 60,000 + 15,000 = 75,000.
Step 2: Xavier sacrifices 1/5, so 75,000 × 1/5 = 15,000 (Yamini Dr., Xavier Cr.). So ₹15,000.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A profit on revaluation at the time of a change in ratio is shared in the new ratio, because the partners will share future profits in that ratio.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The rise or fall in values happened before the change, while the old ratio applied, so it is shared in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the workmen compensation claim is more than the workmen compensation reserve, the excess of the claim is debited to the revaluation account.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The reserve meets the claim as far as it goes; the uncovered part is a loss of the old-ratio period, so it is a revaluation debit.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the market value of investments is higher than their book value, the whole investment fluctuation reserve goes to the partners in the old ratio and the rise in value is credited to the revaluation account.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** No fall needs to be met, so the full reserve is free for the partners, and the increase in the asset is a revaluation gain.

questions.stem_md: A fall in the market value of investments is first met out of the ___.
questions.solution_md: The investment fluctuation reserve absorbs the fall first; any excess fall is a revaluation loss.

questions.stem_md: The revaluation account is a ___ account, closed by transferring its balance to the partners.
questions.solution_md: It records gains and losses, so it is a nominal account.

questions.stem_md: When a workmen compensation claim is expected, the amount of the claim is transferred from the workmen compensation reserve to a ___ for workmen compensation claim.
questions.solution_md: The claim becomes a liability: Workmen Compensation Reserve A/c Dr. To Provision for Workmen Compensation Claim A/c.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A general reserve appearing in the balance sheet is credited to the partners in their old ratio when the profit-sharing ratio changes.

**Reason (R):** The reserve was built out of profits earned while the old ratio applied.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: profits earned under the old ratio belong to the partners in that ratio.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A loss on revaluation at the time of a change in ratio is borne by the partners in their old ratio.

**Reason (R):** The revaluation account is a real account.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: the fall in values belongs to the old-ratio period. R is false: the revaluation account is a nominal account.

questions.stem_md: Match each item in column I with its treatment on a change in the profit-sharing ratio in column II.

options.text_md: Increase in the value of land
Repair bill not recorded so far
Debit balance of the profit and loss account
General reserve

match_right.text_md: Credited to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
Debited to partners' capital accounts in the old ratio

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Changes in values go through revaluation (gain credited, loss debited); accumulated profits and losses go straight to the partners in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md: Gita and Hari share profits 3 : 2 in an imagined furniture showroom in Mysuru and decide to share 2 : 3 from 1 April 2026. They agree that: land be appreciated by ₹25,000; plant be reduced by ₹12,000; stock be increased by ₹6,000; and an outstanding bill for repairs of ₹4,000 be recorded. Prepare the revaluation account.
questions.solution_md: Gains on the credit side, losses on the debit side; the balance is shared in the old ratio, not the new one.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Dr. — Revaluation Account — Cr.**

| Particulars | ₹ | Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| To Plant | 12,000 | By Land | 25,000 |
| To Outstanding repairs bill | 4,000 | By Stock | 6,000 |
| To Gita's Capital A/c (gain) | 9,000 |  |  |
| To Hari's Capital A/c (gain) | 6,000 |  |  |
| **Total** | **31,000** | **Total** | **31,000** |

Gain ₹15,000 shared in the **old ratio 3 : 2**: Gita ₹9,000, Hari ₹6,000.

marking_scheme.step: Debit side: plant and repairs bill
Gain 15,000 shared 9,000 and 6,000 in old ratio

questions.stem_md: Isha, Jay and Kriti are partners in an imagined bakery chain in Dehradun sharing profits 3 : 2 : 1. They decide to share equally from 1 April 2026. Their balance sheet shows a general reserve of ₹36,000 and a debit balance of ₹12,000 in the profit and loss account. Pass journal entries, if the partners do not want to keep these items in the books.
questions.solution_md: Reserve credited and accumulated loss debited to the capitals in the old ratio.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: Explain why reserves, accumulated profits and the gain or loss on revaluation are shared in the old ratio when partners change their profit-sharing ratio. Give one example.
questions.solution_md: Link each item to the period in which it arose, then show with a small example who would lose otherwise.

1. Reserves and accumulated profits were **earned before** the change, while the **old ratio** applied, so they belong to the partners in that ratio.
